newsitem.title: USA: S.F. Fed's Parry sees flaws in US statistics.
newsitem.headline: S.F. Fed's Parry sees flaws in US statistics.

text.p: Robert Parry, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, on Monday said key U.S. statistics on productivity and consumer prices may not be entirely accurate.

Figures on U.S. productivity have shown a strong performance in the manufacturing sector but weakness in the service sector. Productivity overall has increased at a relatively modest pace of about 1.0 percent a year.
But Parry said he suspected that picture may not be correct.

"I frankly think that productivity is rising faster than the measurements suggest," he said, adding that weakness in the service sector did not seem consistent with efficiency improvements that appear to have taken place in key areas such as financial services.

He noted that if the productivity statistics are understated, that would imply that gross domestic product growth is understated as well. "It would also mean that trend growth is greater than we thought it was."

Parry said productivity growth, which may not be showing up to the full extent in the statistics, may be one reason that prices have remained relatively tame despite a period of strong growth earlier this year.
The San Francisco Fed president said it also appeared that inflation may be overstated in the Consumer Price Index.

A congressionally appointed panel headed by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin has suggested the upward bias in the CPI could be a percentage point or more a year. The group is scheduled to issue a final report on the subject Dec. 1.
